planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; this heirloom-grade open-pollinated release carries the original N-gene root-knot nematode resistance later bred into many modern Southern pepper cultivars, making it a dependable choice for sandy Gulf Coast soils with heavy nematode pressure.

directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 55 degrees F. Mississippi Nemaheart was released by Mississippi State University in 1966 as an open-pollinated pimiento-type pepper bred by recurrent backcrossing into 'Truhart Perfection,' and it remains historically significant as the original source of the dominant N gene that confers resistance to southern, peanut, and tropical root-knot nematodes in modern pepper breeding. Plants are moderately vigorous with heart-shaped, thick-walled sweet fruit that ripens from green to deep red and is well suited to canning, roasting, and pimiento cheese. Because root-knot nematodes are endemic in the sandy, poorly drained soils common across the Gulf Coast, this cultivar performs far more reliably there than standard susceptible pimiento types, though its plants can be somewhat weaker-growing than modern hybrids bred from it.
sources: Mississippi State University Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; released by USDA-ARS in 2009, it combines the classic 'Truhart Perfection' pimiento type with the nematode resistance of Mississippi Nemaheart, giving Gulf South gardeners a higher-yielding nematode-resistant pimiento than older resistant lines.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once the soil has warmed. Truhart-NR was developed by USDA-ARS through a backcross program that introduced the dominant root-knot nematode resistance gene from Mississippi Nemaheart into the 'Truhart Perfection' pimiento background, and it was released in 2009 after field trials showed it outyielding its susceptible parent with heavier, longer, thicker-walled fruit. The blocky, three-lobed pimiento fruit ripens to deep red with sweet, thick flesh suited to fresh eating, roasting, and pimiento cheese. It is particularly valuable for organic and specialty growers along the Gulf Coast who lack easy access to chemical nematicides and garden in nematode-infested sandy soils.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service, U.S. Vegetable Laboratory (Charleston, SC)

planting.note: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; released by USDA-ARS in 2006 as the first commercial habanero with root-knot nematode resistance, it is well suited to the sandy, nematode-prone soils common along the Gulf Coast.

directions: Germinate on a heat mat at 80-90 degrees F and transplant outdoors only after nights stay reliably warm. TigerPaw-NR was released by USDA-ARS in 2006 after a recurrent backcross program moved a dominant root-knot nematode resistance gene from a Scotch Bonnet accession into a habanero-type line, producing the first commercially available habanero cultivar resistant to southern, peanut, and tropical root-knot nematodes. Plants are compact and productive, bearing attractive lantern-shaped orange fruit that is extremely pungent, in the same fiery range as standard habaneros. The resistance package makes it a strong choice for home gardeners and small-scale growers along the Gulf Coast, where nematode pressure in light, sandy soils often stunts unprotected habanero plantings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science (HortScience, Vol. 42)
